newsitem.title: USA: U.S. bank reform may set courts as final arbiter.
newsitem.headline: U.S. bank reform may set courts as final arbiter.

text.p: Legislators working to reform U.S. financial laws discussed on Friday using the federal courts, instead of a new council of state and federal regulators, to resolve future disputes arising between banks and insurance companies.

At a hearing on the financial modernization bill, members of the House Commerce Committee debated various approaches for handling such conflicts, which could arise from the legislation's functional regulation provisions.
If the bill were to become law, then banks, insurance companies and securities firms could enter each other's businesses.

Each activity would be regulated by the agency that oversees the activity currently. Banking and securities are regulated at both the state and federal levels, while insurance is regulated solely by states.

But disputes are likely to arise over hybrid products and services that may include elements of both traditional banking and insurance products. Banks want federal bank regulators to have the power to determine what falls under bank rules, while insurance companies want state insurance regulators to determine what is an insurance product.

The reform bill, narrowly approved by the House Banking Committee last month, would send those disputes to a new national council composed of federal bank and securities regulators along with some state regulators and the Secretary of the Treasury.
Members of the commerce committee, which has until mid-September to rework the bill, have expressed significant concerns about the council.

Lobbyists who have met with committee staff in the past week said the staffers were not interested in hearing comments on improving the council. "It sounds like they are just throwing it out," one lobbyist said.
Rep. Mike Oxley, chairman of the committee's finance subcommittee that held Friday's hearing, said the council could be replaced with an expedited review process in the federal courts.

"If the council established in (the bill) is replaced with some form of expedited review in federal courts, this committee must determine what guidance the court should be given," the Ohio Republican said. Such guidance might spell out how much deference the court should accord to the various regulators.
Insurance companies were generally opposed to the council. Jerry Roach, president of the Mutual Assurance Society of Virginia, said his company favored a court proceeding.

"The hearing and ruling by the council on banking-insurance disputes is a time consuming hurdle that must be passed before the parties can access the courts, the proper and ultimate arbiter of such issues," Roach told lawmakers.
Insurance companies also asked that the courts be instructed to give equal weight to the views of state insurance regulators and bank regulators.

The Supreme Court has ruled that federal agencies should be given deference in interpreting the federal laws they oversee. Much to the dismay of the insurance industry, the court allowed the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency to use the National Bank Act to overrule certain state insurance laws as applied to banks.
Rep Rick Lazio, Republican of New York, noted that the courts might be overwhelmed since each of the 50 states would be able to define insurance products under the bill.
"Aren't we sort of inviting an endless stream of litigation if we have this sort of proceeding," he asked.

Lazio also said rapid changes in the market might overtake any legislative solution. "It's my sense that the way these products are evolving to meet global demands will make many of these discussions moot in 10 years," he said.

Even if the Commerce Committee approves the bill, the legislation has an uncertain outlook. Congress has been working to reform the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act for over a decade, but the efforts have always broken down when the various financial industries failed to reach a consensus about key provisions.
